practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'decomposition'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a correct meaning: breaking a large or complex problem down into smaller sub-problems (that are easier to solve). No mark for simply repeating the word without explaining it.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by the term 'abstraction'.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: 1 mark for 'removing or hiding unnecessary detail'; 1 mark for 'so you can focus on / keep the important information needed to solve the problem'. An example (such as a map or a variable name) can earn the second mark if the definition is otherwise incomplete.

practice_questions.text: A developer is planning a new mobile game. Describe how decomposition could help them plan the project.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 3: the game is broken into smaller sub-problems such as graphics, scoring or controls; each part is easier to solve and test on its own; the work can be shared between a team; a solved part can be reused elsewhere. The answer should link back to the game scenario.

practice_questions.text: A navigation app shows drivers the route between two places. Explain how abstraction is used in the design of this app.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks for developed points, for example: the map hides unnecessary detail such as individual buildings or exact terrain (1) so the driver sees only the roads, junctions and turnings they need (1); this makes the route clearer and easier to follow (1); real distances or scale may be simplified while the correct order of turns is kept (1). Credit clear application to the app.

practice_questions.text: A team is building a system to manage borrowing and returning books in a school library. Explain how abstraction, decomposition and algorithmic thinking could each be applied to this problem.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: All three principles clearly explained and applied to the library system with accurate examples. Secure: All three principles correctly identified with mostly clear application to the scenario. Developing: Two principles explained, or all three named with limited application. Emerging: One principle described, or definitions given with no application to the library.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the benefits of using computational thinking techniques when developing a large software project.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced, well-structured discussion covering abstraction, decomposition and algorithmic thinking, with clear reasoning about benefits (such as simpler problems, teamwork, reuse and fewer errors) and a supported judgement. Secure: Clear discussion of the techniques with relevant benefits and some reasoning. Developing: Some benefits given but points are undeveloped, or only one or two techniques covered. Emerging: A few basic points with little explanation, or mostly just definitions.

practice_questions.text: State the purpose of the CPU in a computer system.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that the CPU processes (carries out) the instructions of a program.

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the Control Unit within the CPU.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks. Creditable points: it decodes instructions to work out what must happen (1); it sends out control signals that coordinate and direct the other components (1). Secure: two clear, linked points. Developing: one relevant point. Emerging: a vague reference to controlling the CPU.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens during the fetch stage of the fetch-execute cycle.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: the Program Counter holds the address of the next instruction (1); the instruction is copied from memory into the CPU (1); the Program Counter is then increased so it points to the following instruction (1). Secure: a clear, ordered description. Developing: two correct points. Emerging: one relevant point.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between the Memory Address Register (MAR) and the Memory Data Register (MDR).
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks, up to 2 per register. The MAR holds an address (1) of the memory location the CPU wants to read from or write to (1); the MDR holds data or an instruction (1) that has just been read from, or is about to be written to, memory (1). Secure: both registers explained with the address-versus-data distinction clear. Developing: one register explained, or both stated without expansion. Emerging: a single relevant point.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the CPU uses its registers and the ALU to carry out an instruction during the fetch-execute cycle.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a clear, well-sequenced explanation that the Program Counter provides the address of the next instruction, that the instruction is fetched from memory, that the Control Unit decodes it, and that during execution the ALU performs any calculation with the result placed in the Accumulator before the cycle repeats. Secure: most of these steps explained in a sensible order with correct component and register roles. Developing: some correct steps but gaps or muddled order. Emerging: knows a few components but cannot link them into the cycle.

practice_questions.text: A computer runs a program made up of many instructions. Discuss how the components of the CPU and the fetch-execute cycle work together to carry out this program.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a sustained discussion covering the purpose of the CPU (processing instructions), the roles of the ALU, Control Unit, cache and registers, the storage of instructions and data together under Von Neumann architecture, and the way the fetch, decode and execute stages repeat for each instruction to run the whole program. Secure: several relevant, connected points covering both the components and the cycle. Developing: some correct points but limited linking or one-sided coverage. Emerging: isolated, partly correct points with no clear reasoning.

practice_questions.text: State one reason why a programmer designs an algorithm before writing program code.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for a valid reason. Accept: it helps find logic errors early; it is quicker and cheaper to change a plan than finished code; it makes the required steps clear before coding begins.

practice_questions.text: A program asks the user for two numbers and displays their total. Describe the inputs, the process and the output for this program.
practice_questions.marks: Up to two marks. One mark for correctly identifying the inputs as the two numbers entered by the user. One mark for stating the process and output: add the two numbers together and display the total on screen.

practice_questions.text:
Complete the pseudocode below so that it keeps asking for a password until the user enters the word letmein. Write the three missing parts (marked ___):

password = ___
while password ___ "letmein"
    password = input("Try again: ")
___
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each correct part. First blank: an input statement such as input("Enter password: "). Second blank: the not-equal condition, written as != or 'is not equal to'. Third blank: endwhile. Accept minor variations in syntax.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a trace table can help a programmer find an error in an algorithm that contains a loop.
practice_questions.marks: Indicative content: a trace table has a column for each variable and output; the programmer works through the algorithm by hand, one step at a time; the values are recorded after each pass of the loop; comparing the recorded values with the expected values reveals the exact step where the logic goes wrong. Mastering: clear, accurate explanation that links the table's step-by-step values to locating the error. Secure: correct explanation of how values are tracked to find a fault. Developing: describes what a trace table is with a limited link to finding errors. Emerging: a basic or partly correct point.

practice_questions.text: A shop gives a 10% discount on any order that comes to more than £50. Write an algorithm, using pseudocode or a flowchart, that asks for the order total, works out the amount to pay, and displays it.
practice_questions.marks: Indicative content: input the order total; use selection to test whether the total is more than 50; if it is, reduce the total by 10% (for example multiply by 0.9); output the amount to pay; steps in a sensible order. Mastering: a complete, correct algorithm with correct selection and calculation, clearly presented. Secure: a mostly correct algorithm with only a minor slip. Developing: some correct structure but the selection or the calculation is flawed. Emerging: fragments of a solution only.

practice_questions.text: Compare pseudocode and flowcharts as tools for designing algorithms. In your answer, describe what each one is and explain when a programmer might choose one rather than the other.
practice_questions.marks: Indicative content: pseudocode is code-like English that does not follow strict syntax and is quick to write and easy to translate into real code; a flowchart is a diagram of labelled boxes joined by arrows that makes the order of steps, decisions and loops easy to see; pseudocode suits longer designs and programmers comfortable with code, while a flowchart suits explaining a design visually or showing branching clearly; both express the same sequence, selection and iteration. Mastering: a balanced comparison that accurately describes both tools and justifies when each is preferable. Secure: both tools described correctly with a clear reason for choosing one. Developing: both tools mentioned but the comparison is thin or one description is weak. Emerging: one tool described with little or no comparison.

practice_questions.text: State one characteristic of a CPU that affects its performance.
practice_questions.marks: Accept any one of: clock speed; cache size; number of cores. One clearly named characteristic is enough for full credit.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by the clock speed of a CPU.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clearly states that clock speed is the number of cycles (or instructions) the CPU carries out per second, and names the unit (hertz/gigahertz). Secure: Identifies clock speed as cycles per second, measured in hertz or gigahertz. Developing: Vague link to how fast the CPU runs without naming cycles or the unit. Emerging: Little relevant detail or a confused idea of speed.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the size of a CPU's cache can affect its performance.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that cache stores frequently used data and instructions close to the CPU, that a larger cache holds more of this data, giving more cache hits and fewer slow fetches from RAM, so the CPU works faster. Secure: Links a larger cache to more cache hits or fewer trips to RAM and therefore better performance. Developing: States that more cache is better without explaining cache hits or the link to RAM. Emerging: Names cache but gives no valid effect on performance.

practice_questions.text: Explain how increasing the number of cores can improve the performance of a CPU.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that each core can run the fetch-execute cycle independently, so several cores allow parallel processing where different instructions run at the same time, increasing the amount of work done per second, and notes this depends on software being able to share the work. Secure: Links extra cores to parallel processing and more instructions handled at once, giving better performance. Developing: States more cores are faster with a partial reason. Emerging: Simple statement that more cores help, with no explanation.

practice_questions.text: Two laptops have the same clock speed. Laptop A has a larger cache but Laptop B has more cores. Compare how each design could affect performance for different tasks.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced comparison. Explains that Laptop A's larger cache gives more cache hits and fewer slow fetches from RAM, helping tasks that reuse the same data; explains that Laptop B's extra cores allow parallel processing, helping when running several programs or multi-threaded software; concludes that the better choice depends on the workload. Secure: Describes a clear benefit of both designs and links each to suitable tasks. Developing: Describes one design well but the other only briefly, or omits the task link. Emerging: States differences with little or no link to performance.

practice_questions.text: A student wants to upgrade their computer so that it runs demanding video-editing software much more quickly. Discuss the CPU characteristics they should consider and how each would affect performance.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained discussion of all three characteristics. Clock speed raises the number of cycles per second; a larger cache reduces slow fetches from RAM; more cores enable parallel processing, which suits video editing if the software is multi-threaded. Weighs the characteristics against each other, notes trade-offs such as heat and power, and reaches a justified conclusion about the most useful upgrade. Secure: Discusses at least two characteristics with correct effects and gives a reasoned recommendation. Developing: Describes characteristics with some correct effects but limited discussion or judgement. Emerging: Lists characteristics with little explanation of their effect on performance.

practice_questions.text: State the one condition that a data set must meet before a binary search can be carried out.
practice_questions.marks: Correct response: the data must be sorted (arranged in order, such as ascending or descending). Accept any wording showing the list is ordered, for example 'in alphabetical order' or 'smallest to largest'.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a linear search finds a value in a list.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: the search starts at the first item and compares it with the target; if it does not match it moves on to the next item, repeating until the target is found or the end of the list is reached. Developing: mentions checking items one at a time from the start but leaves out how the search ends. Emerging: a vague reference to looking through the list.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a binary search cannot be used to find a value in the list: 14, 3, 27, 8, 19.
practice_questions.marks: Secure response covers: the list is not sorted (1); a binary search relies on the order of the data to decide which half to keep and which half to discard (1); on unsorted data the discarded half might actually contain the target, so the search could miss it or give the wrong result (1). Developing: identifies that the list is unsorted with a partial reason. Emerging: states only that the list is not in order.

practice_questions.text: Compare a linear search and a binary search. Refer to how each one works and how efficient they are.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a clear, balanced comparison covering both how each search works (linear checks items in turn from the start; binary checks the middle and discards half) and their efficiency (binary is far faster on large lists but needs sorted data; linear works on any order). Secure: describes both methods with at least one clear comparison of efficiency or requirements. Developing: describes both methods but with little direct comparison. Emerging: an isolated point about one method.

practice_questions.text: A shopping website stores a list of 5,000 product codes that is always kept in order. Discuss which searching algorithm the developers should use to look up a product code, and justify your choice.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a well-reasoned recommendation of a binary search, justified by its efficiency on a large list (halving the data each pass means only a handful of comparisons for 5,000 items) and by the fact that the list is already sorted, so the prerequisite is met; may weigh this against a linear search to strengthen the argument. Secure: recommends binary search with a clear efficiency reason and notes the list is sorted. Developing: makes a choice with a basic reason. Emerging: names a search with little or no justification.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of a linear search and a binary search, and explain the situations in which each one is the better choice.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a balanced discussion covering the strengths and weaknesses of both methods (linear: simple, works on unsorted data, but slow on long lists; binary: very fast on large lists, but requires sorted data which itself takes time to produce) and links these to clear situations where each is preferable, such as small or frequently changing data for linear and large, stable, sorted data for binary. Secure: covers advantages and disadvantages of both with at least one appropriate situation for each. Developing: covers both methods but the discussion is one-sided or the situations are unclear. Emerging: a few isolated points with little development.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term embedded system.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: identifies that it is a computer built into a larger device to perform one dedicated task. Developing: describes it loosely as a small computer inside a device. Emerging: gives only an example without any definition.

practice_questions.text: Give two typical characteristics of an embedded system.
practice_questions.marks: Answers may include: dedicated to a single task; small in size; low power consumption; low cost; highly reliable; real-time response. Secure: two clear, distinct characteristics. Developing: one valid characteristic, or two that overlap. Emerging: vague or repeated points.

practice_questions.text: Identify two devices, other than a washing machine, that contain an embedded system.
practice_questions.marks: Answers may include: microwave, dishwasher, central-heating thermostat, traffic lights, digital camera, car engine-management or braking system, pacemaker, fitness tracker, MP3 player. Secure: two suitable dedicated-function devices. Developing: one suitable device. Emerging: names a general-purpose computer such as a laptop.

practice_questions.text: Describe why an embedded system is usually built around a microcontroller.
practice_questions.marks: Answers may include: a microcontroller combines the processor, memory and input/output on one chip; this keeps the device small and cheap; it provides just enough power for the single task; the firmware is held in read-only memory so it is ready at switch-on. Secure: three linked points. Developing: one or two relevant points. Emerging: a single vague statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons a manufacturer might choose an embedded system rather than a general-purpose computer inside a product.
practice_questions.marks: Answers may include, with justification: lower cost (mass-produced, only the needed hardware); smaller size (fits inside the product); lower power use; greater reliability (less to go wrong); real-time response to inputs. Mastering: two reasons each clearly explained with a consequence. Secure: two reasons with some explanation. Developing: reasons identified but not explained. Emerging: one weak or incorrect point.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the differences between an embedded system and a general-purpose computer, using examples of each.
practice_questions.marks: Answers should contrast: dedicated single function vs running many programs; fixed firmware vs user-installable software; limited, task-matched resources vs plenty of memory and storage; hard to upgrade vs easily upgraded; with examples such as a microwave controller vs a laptop. Mastering: a balanced, well-organised comparison across several points with apt examples. Secure: a clear comparison of several differences with at least one example. Developing: some valid differences but limited detail or examples. Emerging: isolated points with little comparison.

practice_questions.text: Which statement best describes how bubble sort works? A) It splits the list in half and merges the pieces back together. B) It compares adjacent items and swaps any that are in the wrong order. C) It builds a sorted section at the front by inserting each new item. D) It checks the middle item and discards half of the list each time.
practice_questions.marks: Correct answer: B (bubble sort compares adjacent items and swaps those in the wrong order). 1 mark. A describes merge sort, C describes insertion sort, D describes a search method rather than a sort.

practice_questions.text: State what merge sort does to the list before it begins merging any items back together.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that it repeatedly splits/divides the list in half until each sub-list contains a single item. Accept 'breaks the list down into individual items'.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens during a single pass of bubble sort.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per valid point to a maximum of 2. Points: it moves through the list comparing each pair of adjacent items; it swaps a pair whenever they are in the wrong order (larger before smaller for ascending). Secure: both compare and conditional-swap given. Developing: only one point given.

practice_questions.text: Explain why merge sort is usually a better choice than bubble sort for sorting a very large list.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clearly links merge sort's divide-and-conquer approach to far fewer comparisons as the list grows, so it stays fast on large lists, while acknowledging bubble sort's comparisons rise steeply. Secure: states merge sort is faster on large lists because the work grows more gently. Developing: states merge sort is faster without explaining why. Emerging: vague or unsupported statement.

practice_questions.text: Trace a bubble sort on the list 8, 3, 5, 1 sorting into ascending order. Write out the full list after each complete pass until it is sorted.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct pass state, to a maximum of 4. After pass 1: 3, 5, 1, 8. After pass 2: 3, 1, 5, 8. After pass 3: 1, 3, 5, 8. Final pass makes no swaps, confirming the sorted list 1, 3, 5, 8. Mastering: all pass states correct and in order. Developing: some pass states correct with minor slips.

practice_questions.text: Compare bubble sort, insertion sort and merge sort. Refer to how each one works and to how efficient each is, then recommend which you would use to sort a very large list, giving a reason.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: accurate account of all three methods (bubble: swap adjacent pairs over repeated passes; insertion: build a sorted front section by shifting; merge: split then merge halves), a clear efficiency comparison (merge sort scales best on large lists but uses more memory; the simple sorts are easy and in-place but slow on large lists), and a justified recommendation of merge sort for a large list. Secure: describes all three and makes a supported recommendation. Developing: describes some methods with a partial comparison. Emerging: lists methods with little comparison or justification.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'volatile' when it is used to describe computer memory.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that volatile memory loses its contents (data) when the power is switched off.

practice_questions.text: Describe the purpose of RAM in a computer system.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Creditable points include: holds the data, instructions or programs currently in use / holds the running operating system and open applications and files (1); allows the CPU to access these quickly because it can read them directly (1). Secure: two clear, linked points about what RAM does. Developing: one relevant point. Emerging: a vague reference to storing data.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a computer system needs ROM as well as RAM.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks for a linked explanation. Points: RAM is volatile so it is empty when the computer is switched on (1); ROM is non-volatile so it keeps its contents when the power is off (1); ROM therefore stores the start-up (bootstrap) instructions that load the operating system into RAM (1). Secure: a logical chain linking volatility to the need for ROM. Developing: correct facts but not fully linked. Emerging: an isolated point.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between RAM and ROM.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks, up to 2 per difference (1 for the difference, 1 for expansion). Valid differences: volatility (RAM volatile / ROM non-volatile); read-write access (RAM can be read and written / ROM is read only under normal use); contents (RAM holds programs and data in use / ROM holds the start-up instructions); size (RAM is usually larger than ROM). Secure: two clearly explained differences. Developing: one explained difference, or two stated without expansion. Emerging: a single relevant point.

practice_questions.text: Explain how virtual memory allows a computer to keep running when its RAM becomes full.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a clear, well-sequenced explanation that virtual memory sets aside an area of secondary storage to act as extra RAM, that unused data is moved out of RAM to this area to free space, that it is swapped back into RAM when needed, and that this transfer keeps the system running. Secure: most of these steps explained in a sensible order. Developing: some correct steps but gaps or muddled order. Emerging: knows virtual memory uses the hard drive but cannot explain the swapping process.

practice_questions.text: A user complains that their computer becomes very slow when they open a large number of programs at the same time. Discuss the roles of RAM and virtual memory in this situation and suggest how the problem could be improved.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained discussion linking limited RAM to it filling up, the computer resorting to virtual memory on slower secondary storage, the resulting swapping of data between RAM and storage slowing the system, and a justified improvement such as installing more RAM so virtual memory is rarely needed. Secure: several relevant, connected points covering both RAM and virtual memory with a sensible improvement. Developing: some correct points but limited linking or one-sided coverage. Emerging: isolated, partly correct points with no clear reasoning.

practice_questions.text: State the difference between a variable and a constant.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for stating that a variable's value can change while a program runs; one mark for stating that a constant's value is fixed and cannot change while the program runs.

practice_questions.text: Give the value produced by each of these expressions: 23 DIV 4 and 23 MOD 4.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for 23 DIV 4 = 5 (the whole-number quotient). One mark for 23 MOD 4 = 3 (the remainder).

practice_questions.text: A program should welcome a user only when their age is at least 13 and no more than 18. Write a single condition, using comparison and Boolean operators, that is true only for ages in this range.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for a correct lower bound such as age >= 13. One mark for a correct upper bound such as age <= 18. One mark for correctly joining the two with AND, for example age >= 13 AND age <= 18.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the selection construct changes the way a program runs, and give one example of when a program would need it.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear explanation that selection chooses between different blocks of code based on a true or false condition, with a relevant example. Secure: correct explanation of choosing a path from a condition, with a basic example. Developing: partial idea of making a choice; example vague or missing. Emerging: names selection or if statements with little explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a count-controlled loop and a condition-controlled loop. Include an example of a task that suits each one.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: precise explanation that a count-controlled loop repeats a set number of times while a condition-controlled loop repeats until a condition is met, with a fitting example of each. Secure: correct difference explained with at least one suitable example. Developing: some awareness of the difference; examples weak or only one given. Emerging: names the loop types with little or no explanation.

practice_questions.text: A simple quiz program keeps asking the user a question until they type the correct answer, then displays how many attempts they took. Describe how variables, assignment and iteration would work together to build this program.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained answer linking a variable to count attempts, assignment to update it, input to read each guess, and a condition-controlled loop that repeats until the answer is correct, then output of the count. Secure: covers variables, assignment and iteration correctly with a mostly complete description. Developing: mentions some of the parts but with gaps or muddled links between them. Emerging: identifies one or two relevant ideas with little detail.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by secondary storage, and give one reason a computer needs it.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for stating that secondary storage is non-volatile storage that keeps data, programs and the operating system for the long term (even when the power is off). One mark for a valid reason it is needed, such as working memory being volatile, or being too small and expensive to hold everything. Two valid points earn full marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a magnetic hard disk drive stores and reads data.
practice_questions.marks: Up to three marks for a clear description. Creditable points: data is stored as magnetised patterns/areas on spinning platters (1); a read/write head moves across the platter surface to reach the right position (1); the head detects the magnetism to read, or changes it to write, with each magnetised area representing a binary 1 or 0 (1). Any three accurate points gain full marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two advantages of using solid-state storage instead of a magnetic hard disk drive.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each valid advantage identified, plus one mark for developing an advantage with a reason, up to three marks. Valid advantages: faster access, more durable/shock-resistant, silent, lower power use, more compact. A developed point such as “more durable because it has no moving parts to break if the device is dropped” earns the development mark.

practice_questions.text: A wildlife photographer needs storage to carry in the field and copy photos onto during long trips. Recommend a suitable type of secondary storage and justify your choice.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: names a suitable device (such as an SSD or a solid-state memory card / USB flash drive) and justifies it clearly against several relevant characteristics — portability, durability and speed. Secure: names a suitable device with two relevant justifications. Developing: names a suitable device with one basic reason. Emerging: names a device with little or no valid justification.

practice_questions.text: A company must back up several terabytes of data every night and keep copies stored safely off-site. Discuss which type of secondary storage would be most suitable, referring to the characteristics that matter for this situation.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: recommends a suitable type (such as magnetic tape or high-capacity hard disk drives) and discusses it against the key characteristics — very high capacity, low cost per gigabyte, and portability for off-site storage — while weighing the drawback of slow sequential access and explaining why it does not matter for backups. Secure: recommends a suitable type with clear reference to two or three relevant characteristics. Developing: makes a recommendation with some relevant reasoning but limited development. Emerging: names a type with little justification or relevance to the scenario.

practice_questions.text: State the approximate storage capacity of a standard CD and of a single-layer DVD.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for CD approximately 700 MB. One mark for single-layer DVD approximately 4.7 GB. Accept answers close to these values.

practice_questions.text: What is the denary value of the binary number 00101010? A) 21  B) 42  C) 84  D) 168
practice_questions.marks: Correct response: B (42). Secure: adds the place values under each 1 (32 + 8 + 2) to reach 42. Developing or Emerging: selects a value from a miscount of the columns or from doubling or halving the correct answer.

practice_questions.text: Convert the denary number 217 into (a) an 8-bit binary number and (b) a two-digit hexadecimal number.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: (a) 11011001 and (b) D9, both correct with working shown. Developing: one part correct, or the right method with a single place-value slip. Emerging: a partial attempt such as correct place values identified but not combined into the final answer.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a computer adds the two 8-bit binary numbers 00110101 and 00010110 together, and state the final 8-bit result.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering or Secure: describes working from the least significant bit to the most significant bit, carrying a 1 into the next column when two 1s are added, and gives the result 01001011. Developing: describes the carrying process but the final answer is wrong, or gives the right answer with a thin description. Emerging: a vague reference to adding the numbers with no clear method or result.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by an overflow error, and explain why one can occur when a computer adds two 8-bit binary numbers.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: states that an overflow error happens when a result is too large to fit in the available number of bits, and explains that two 8-bit numbers can total more than 255, so the answer needs a ninth bit that cannot be stored and the carry is lost. Secure: correct definition and a mostly clear reason. Developing: correct definition but a weak or missing explanation of the cause. Emerging: only a partial idea, such as 'the number is too big', with no link to the number of bits.

practice_questions.text: A program shifts the 8-bit binary number 00010100 two places to the left. Describe the effect this has on the value and state the resulting 8-bit number.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering or Secure: explains that a left shift multiplies the value by two for each place, so a shift of two places multiplies by four, taking 20 to 80, and gives the result 01010000. Developing: identifies that the value is multiplied but gets the factor or the final number wrong. Emerging: states that the bits move left with no correct explanation of the effect on the value.

practice_questions.text: Compare the ASCII and Unicode character sets. In your answer, refer to the number of bits each uses per character and the range of characters each can represent.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: compares both sets in detail, noting that ASCII uses 7 bits per character and represents 128 characters suited to English, while Unicode uses more bits (commonly 16 or 32) and represents well over a million characters from many languages, and links more bits to larger file sizes. Secure: a clear comparison of bits and character range for both sets. Developing: describes each set separately but the comparison is limited. Emerging: a basic point about one set only, with little or no comparison.

practice_questions.text: Which of the following values would be stored as a real (float)?  A) 42   B) True   C) 3.14   D) 'k'
practice_questions.marks: One mark for C) 3.14, because it is a number that includes a decimal (fractional) part.

practice_questions.text: State the most suitable data type for each of the following: the number of lives a player has left, and whether the player has unlocked the bonus round.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for integer (a whole number) for the number of lives left. One mark for Boolean (True or False) for whether the bonus round is unlocked.

practice_questions.text: A program uses the line total = input("Enter price: ") and then tries to add VAT to total, but it does not work. Explain why casting is needed and how it fixes the problem.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying that input returns a string. One mark for explaining that arithmetic cannot be carried out on a string. One mark for stating that casting the input to a real (or integer) lets the number be used in the calculation.

practice_questions.text: A program needs to store the seven days of the week. Write a line that declares a suitable one-dimensional array, and a line that stores 'Monday' as the first element.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for declaring an array of the correct size, for example array days[7]. One mark for using the correct first index of 0. One mark for a valid assignment, for example days[0] = "Monday".

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between an array and a record, using an example of data that each one is well suited to storing.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear explanation that an array stores many items of the same data type while a record groups related fields that may be different data types, with a fitting example of each. Secure: correct difference with at least one suitable example. Developing: partial difference or only one structure explained; example weak. Emerging: names arrays or records with little explanation.

practice_questions.text: A school wants to store data about its students so a program can process it. Each student has a name, an age, an average grade and whether their fees are paid. Discuss how data types and data structures could be used to store this data effectively.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained answer that selects suitable data types (such as string for name, integer for age, real for average grade, Boolean for fees paid) and explains using a record to group one student's fields and an array to hold many students, with justified choices. Secure: identifies appropriate data types and at least one suitable structure with mostly correct reasoning. Developing: some suitable data types or structures named with limited justification. Emerging: identifies one or two relevant ideas with little detail.

practice_questions.text: How many different colours can be stored using a colour depth of 3 bits? A) 3  B) 6  C) 8  D) 9
practice_questions.marks: Correct response: C (8). Secure: applies the rule that n bits store 2 to the power of n colours, so 3 bits give 2 cubed = 8. Developing or Emerging: multiplies the bits (for example 3 × 2 = 6) or misreads the doubling rule, showing it is not yet secure.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'sample rate' and state the unit in which it is measured.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: defines sample rate as the number of samples (measurements of the sound wave) taken each second, and correctly gives the unit as Hertz (Hz). Developing: correct definition but the unit is missing or wrong. Emerging: only a vague idea such as 'how fast the sound plays', with no unit.

practice_questions.text: Describe how an analogue sound wave is converted so that it can be stored in digital form on a computer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering or Secure: explains that the wave is sampled — its amplitude is measured at regular intervals — and that each measurement is stored as a binary number, noting that more samples per second give a more accurate recording. Developing: mentions sampling but gives only one or two of these points. Emerging: states that the sound is turned into binary without describing how sampling works.

practice_questions.text: An image is 50 pixels wide and 40 pixels high with a colour depth of 4 bits. Calculate the size of the image file in bits. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: multiplies colour depth × width × height (4 × 50 × 40) to reach 8,000 bits, with clear working shown. Developing: uses the correct method but makes an arithmetic slip, or gives 8,000 bits with no working. Emerging: recalls the formula but does not substitute the values correctly.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of increasing an image's colour depth on both the quality of the image and the size of its file.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains that a greater colour depth means more bits per pixel, so more colours (2 to the power of the colour depth) can be shown, improving quality and giving smoother shading; and that because each pixel now uses more bits, the overall file size increases. Secure: makes both the quality point and the file-size point with some reasoning. Developing: covers only one of the two effects, or states both without reasons. Emerging: a vague comment such as 'it looks better' with no link to bits or file size.

practice_questions.text: A music streaming service must choose the sample rate and bit depth for the songs it stores. Discuss the factors its developers should weigh up when balancing sound quality against file size.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: discusses both sides — a higher sample rate and bit depth capture the wave more accurately for better playback quality, but they multiply the file size (sample rate × duration × bit depth), using more storage and download data; and reaches a justified conclusion about a sensible balance. Secure: covers the quality and file-size effects with some justification. Developing: describes one effect clearly but the discussion stays one-sided. Emerging: a few basic points with no real weighing of the two factors.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a function and a procedure.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: clearly states that a function returns a value to the part of the program that called it, whereas a procedure carries out a task but returns no value. Developing: identifies that only one of them returns a value but explains the point loosely. Emerging: names functions and procedures without making the return-value distinction clear.

practice_questions.text: A program uses a sub program to calculate the area of a rectangle. Explain what parameters are and how this sub program would use them.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: defines a parameter as a variable in the sub program definition that receives an incoming value, and explains that the width and height would be passed in as parameters so the sub program can calculate the area of any rectangle. Developing: gives a partial definition of a parameter and links it loosely to width and height. Emerging: mentions passing numbers in without correctly using the idea of a parameter.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a local variable and a global variable, and give one advantage of using local variables.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: accurately distinguishes a local variable (exists only inside the sub program where it is created) from a global variable (accessible anywhere in the program) and gives a clear advantage, such as a local variable cannot be changed accidentally by other parts of the program, which reduces errors. Secure: correct distinction with a valid advantage stated more simply. Developing: distinction is only partly correct or the advantage is vague. Emerging: confuses the two terms or gives no valid advantage.

practice_questions.text: Write a few lines of pseudocode that open a text file called scores.txt, write the line "Pass" to it, and then close the file.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: pseudocode stores the opened file in a variable, uses a writeLine command to add the text "Pass", and closes the file, for example open("scores.txt") then myFile.writeLine("Pass") then myFile.close(). Developing: two of the three operations are correct, or the file is not stored in a variable. Emerging: only one operation is attempted correctly.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by the scope of a variable.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: explains that scope means the parts of a program in which a variable can be used or accessed, and shows understanding that some variables are only usable within a particular sub program. Developing: gives a partial idea of scope, such as where a variable works, without full clarity. Emerging: restates the word scope without explaining it.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the benefits of using sub programs to produce structured code that is easy to maintain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained discussion covering several clear benefits — writing a block of code once and calling it many times avoids repetition, small named blocks are easier to read and test, work can be shared between programmers, and local variables keep each sub program independent — with reasoning that links each benefit to maintainability. Secure: several valid benefits explained with some development. Developing: a couple of relevant benefits stated with limited explanation. Emerging: one simple benefit with little or no development.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term input validation.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for a correct statement, e.g. automatic checks that test whether entered data is sensible or allowable before the program processes it. Accept: reasonable / acceptable / within set limits.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'anticipating misuse' as part of defensive design.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying that the programmer predicts how a user might enter wrong data or try to break the program; one mark for saying the program is then written to handle those situations safely rather than crash. Example (blank field, letters instead of a number, impossible value) may earn a mark. Secure: both points made clearly. Developing: one point only.

practice_questions.text: A program asks a user to enter their age in whole years. Describe two validation checks that could be applied to this input, and state what each one would reject.
practice_questions.marks: Up to three marks. One mark for each correctly named and described check (e.g. presence check rejects an empty box; type check rejects letters/decimals; range check rejects an age below 0 or above a sensible upper limit). A third mark for a clear example of a rejected input. Secure: two checks named with what each rejects. Developing: one valid check, or checks named without saying what they reject.

practice_questions.text: Explain how authentication helps to make a login system more secure. Refer to one example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear explanation that authentication confirms the user's identity before granting access, with a developed example (e.g. a username identifies the claim and a password proves it, or two-factor authentication adds a code sent to a phone) and why this blocks unauthorised users. Secure: correct purpose plus a relevant example. Developing: partial idea, such as naming a method without explaining how it improves security. Emerging: vague reference to passwords with no explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe two techniques a programmer can use to make a program easier to maintain, explaining how each technique helps.
practice_questions.marks: Up to four marks: two marks per technique (one for naming it, one for explaining the benefit). Valid techniques: sub programs (avoid repeated code / fix a bug in one place), naming conventions (self-explanatory identifiers), indentation (shows code structure), commenting (explains code to future programmers). Secure: two techniques with a correct benefit each. Developing: techniques named without a clear benefit.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how defensive design and input validation can be used to make a program that stores new user accounts robust and secure.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a balanced discussion linking several ideas — anticipating misuse (blank or oversized entries), a range of validation checks on each field (presence, length and format on a password; format on an email), authentication for returning users, strong-password rules enforced by length and format checks, and maintainable code so the system can be fixed safely. Points are justified with clear reasons. Secure: several relevant techniques described with some justification. Developing: a few valid techniques listed with limited explanation. Emerging: one or two isolated points with little development.

practice_questions.text: Identify which one of these file formats uses lossless compression: JPEG, MP3, PNG or MP4.
practice_questions.marks: Correct response: PNG. Secure: identifies PNG as the lossless format that stores an image without discarding data. Developing or Emerging: selects a lossy format (JPEG, MP3 or MP4), showing the lossless and lossy distinction is not yet secure.

practice_questions.text: State two reasons why a large file might need to be compressed before it is sent over a network.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: states two valid reasons, such as reducing the time taken to transfer the file and using less bandwidth or storage space. Developing: states one valid reason. Emerging: gives a vague answer that is not a genuine reason to compress a file.

practice_questions.text: Describe how lossless compression is able to reduce the size of a file without losing any information.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: describes that lossless compression finds redundancy (repeated or predictable data) and records it more efficiently, so the process can be reversed to rebuild the original exactly. Developing: makes one or two relevant points, for example that no data is lost, but the mechanism is unclear. Emerging: states only that the file becomes smaller, with no valid explanation of how.

practice_questions.text: A student wants to email a folder containing a coursework document and several holiday photos. Explain why the document should be compressed using a lossless method while the photos could be compressed using a lossy method.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains that the document must keep every character because losing data could corrupt the text, so lossless is required, while the photos can lose fine detail the eye barely notices, so lossy gives a much larger size saving at little cost. Secure: makes the correct choice for each file with some justification. Developing: correct choices but weak or one-sided reasoning. Emerging: identifies one appropriate method without a clear reason.

practice_questions.text: Explain the main advantages and disadvantages of using lossy compression rather than lossless compression for storing a large music library.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains that lossy compression makes each track far smaller, so many more songs fit in the same storage and they stream faster, but that some audio detail is permanently lost and quality falls if the file is heavily compressed or re-saved, whereas lossless would preserve full quality at the cost of much larger files. Secure: gives clear advantages and disadvantages with some development. Developing: states an advantage or a disadvantage with limited explanation. Emerging: a basic point about size or quality only.

practice_questions.text: A photographer keeps original photographs and also uploads smaller versions to a website. Discuss the factors they should consider when choosing between lossy and lossless compression for each of these two purposes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: discusses both purposes in a balanced way — the master copies should be kept lossless (or uncompressed) so no detail is lost and future edits stay sharp, while the website versions can be lossy to reduce file size, speed up page loading and save bandwidth, accepting a small and hard-to-notice drop in quality — and weighs the trade-off between file size, image quality and whether the original can be recovered. Secure: considers both purposes and the main trade-offs with clear reasoning. Developing: makes relevant points about one purpose, or lists advantages without applying them to the scenario. Emerging: basic points about compression with little link to the photographer's needs.

practice_questions.text: Identify the type of network that covers a small geographical area on a single site, such as a school.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for correctly naming a Local Area Network (LAN). Secure: the correct term is given. Emerging: a vague or incorrect answer, such as 'the internet', earns nothing.

practice_questions.text: State two factors that can affect the performance of a network.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks, one for each correct factor. Secure: identifies two valid factors, such as the available bandwidth and the number of devices connected. Developing: gives one valid factor. Emerging: no valid factor given. Other acceptable factors include the type of transmission media and the level of interference.

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the DNS when a user types a web address into a browser.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clearly describes that the DNS is made up of many domain name servers and converts the typed web address into the IP address of the server, which the browser then connects to. Secure: states that the DNS converts a domain name into an IP address. Developing: shows partial understanding, for example that the DNS helps find a website. Emerging: little or no accurate detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using a star topology for a school network.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains one clear advantage (for example, if one cable fails only that device is affected, or each device has a dedicated connection giving good performance) and one clear disadvantage (for example, if the central switch fails the whole network stops, or a lot of cabling is required), with reasoning for each. Secure: gives an advantage and a disadvantage with some explanation. Developing: identifies an advantage or a disadvantage without full explanation. Emerging: a vague or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: A business wants its staff to reach the same files and software from home as well as in the office. Explain how cloud computing could meet this need, and describe one drawback the business should consider.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains that the cloud provides storage, software and processing remotely over the internet, so staff can reach the same files and applications from any location with an internet connection, and clearly describes a drawback such as dependence on a reliable internet connection, ongoing subscription costs, or concerns about the security of data held by a third party. Secure: explains the benefit of remote access and gives a relevant drawback. Developing: shows some understanding of the cloud but limited explanation. Emerging: little accurate understanding of cloud computing.

practice_questions.text: A small office is choosing between wired and wireless connections for its network. Discuss the benefits and drawbacks of each option and recommend which the office should choose.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: discusses wired connections (faster, more stable, and more secure because physical access is needed, but less flexible and costlier to install) and wireless connections (convenient and mobile, easy to add devices, but generally slower, prone to interference and easier to intercept), weighs them against the needs of a small office, and reaches a justified recommendation. Secure: gives benefits and drawbacks of both options and makes a recommendation. Developing: covers one option well, or both briefly, with a limited judgement. Emerging: a few disconnected points with little or no comparison. Well-organised writing that uses accurate technical terms strengthens the response.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a logic error.
practice_questions.marks: Credit a correct meaning: an error where the program runs but produces unexpected or incorrect output. Do not credit answers that instead describe a syntax error (breaking the rules of the language).

practice_questions.text: Define the terms 'iterative testing' and 'final testing'.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each correct definition. Iterative testing: testing small parts or modules repeatedly as they are written during development. Final (terminal) testing: testing the whole finished program at the end to check all the parts work together.

practice_questions.text: A program accepts a person's age, which must be a whole number from 11 to 16. Describe suitable normal, boundary and erroneous test data for this program, giving one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each type paired with a valid example. Normal: a typical accepted value such as 13. Boundary: a value on the edge of the range such as 11 or 16 (accept 10 or 17 as just-outside boundary values). Erroneous: data of the wrong type such as the word 'twelve' or a symbol.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between invalid test data and erroneous test data. Use an example to support each answer.
practice_questions.marks: Invalid data is of the correct data type but should be rejected because it is out of range (e.g. an age of 40 when the range is 11 to 16). Erroneous data is of the incorrect data type and should be rejected (e.g. entering 'ten' as text). Credit a clear distinction based on data type plus a correct example for each.

practice_questions.text: A program runs without crashing but gives the wrong answer. Explain why a programmer would use a trace table to investigate.
practice_questions.marks: Response should recognise this is a logic error, so no error message appears to point at the fault. A trace table lets the programmer follow the code line by line and record how each variable changes, then compare the actual values against the expected values to pinpoint where the program goes wrong. Credit clear reasoning linking the technique to locating logic errors.

practice_questions.text: Compare syntax errors and logic errors. In your answer, refer to how each type of error affects whether a program runs and how a programmer would find each one.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained comparison making clear that a syntax error breaks the language rules and stops the program being translated or run (usually flagged with a line number), while a logic error lets the program run but produces wrong output and must be found by tracing or dry running; differences in detection are drawn out throughout. Secure: Clear explanation of both error types and at least one clear difference in how each is found. Developing: Some accurate points about each error type with limited comparison. Emerging: Simple, isolated points; little or no comparison between the two.

practice_questions.text: Which one of the following is an example of social engineering? A) Ransomware  B) Phishing  C) A denial of service attack  D) SQL injection
practice_questions.marks: Correct response: B (Phishing). Secure: identifies phishing as social engineering because it manipulates a person into handing over information rather than attacking the technology directly. Developing or Emerging: selects a technical attack such as SQL injection or a denial of service attack, which target systems rather than people.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by a brute-force attack.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: describes a brute-force attack as an attacker trying many possible passwords or combinations, one after another, until the correct one is found, usually automated by software. Developing: a partial description such as 'guessing a password' without the idea of trying many systematically. Emerging: names the attack but does not describe how it works.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a firewall helps to protect a computer network from attack.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering or Secure: explains that a firewall sits between the network and the outside, checks incoming and outgoing traffic against a set of rules, and blocks anything suspicious or unauthorised, so attacks and unwanted connections are stopped before they reach devices. Developing: states that a firewall blocks traffic but does not explain the rule-checking or its position between the network and the outside. Emerging: identifies the firewall as protection with no explanation of how it works.

practice_questions.text: A small business is worried about malware infecting its computers. Explain two prevention methods it could use to reduce this threat.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains two suitable methods (for example anti-malware software that scans for and removes malicious code, and user access levels or staff training that reduce risky behaviour) and links each clearly to reducing the malware threat. Secure: two valid methods with some explanation of how each helps. Developing: two methods named with weak explanation, or one method explained well. Emerging: names a method with little or no explanation.

practice_questions.text: A company allows staff to log in to its network from home. Discuss the threats this creates and the methods the company could use to keep its data secure.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: discusses relevant threats (such as data interception on insecure connections, brute-force attacks on weak passwords, and phishing aimed at remote staff) and balances them against appropriate prevention methods (encryption of data in transit, strong passwords, firewalls and staff training), with clear reasoning linking each method to the threat it addresses. Secure: covers several threats and prevention methods with mostly clear links. Developing: lists some threats and methods but the links between them are limited. Emerging: a few relevant points with little development or connection.

practice_questions.text: A secondary school stores students' personal data on its network. Discuss the main threats to this data and evaluate the prevention methods the school could put in place to protect it.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: gives a balanced, well-structured discussion covering a range of threats (malware, social engineering such as phishing, brute-force attacks, data interception and SQL injection) and evaluates a matching range of prevention methods (penetration testing, anti-malware, firewalls, user access levels, strong passwords, encryption and physical security), judging how effective each is and reaching a supported conclusion. Secure: covers several threats and prevention methods with clear explanation and some evaluation. Developing: describes threats and methods but with limited evaluation or structure. Emerging: a few relevant points with little development, evaluation or link between threat and defence.

practice_questions.text: State the output produced by a NOT gate when its input is 0.
practice_questions.marks: Correct answer: 1 (also accept 'true' or 'on'). A NOT gate inverts its input, so an input of 0 produces an output of 1.

practice_questions.text: A logic circuit uses a single OR gate with inputs A and B. Complete a truth table showing the output Q for all four possible combinations of inputs.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: all four output values correct — Q is 0 only when A is 0 and B is 0, and Q is 1 for the other three combinations. Developing: two or three output values correct. Emerging: fewer than two correct, or missing input combinations.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between the behaviour of an AND gate and an OR gate.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: clearly states that an AND gate outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1, whereas an OR gate outputs 1 when at least one input is 1. Developing: one gate described correctly, the other vague or missing. Emerging: a partly incorrect or muddled description of both gates.

practice_questions.text: A door alarm sounds (output Q = 1) only when the door sensor (A) is triggered AND the system is armed (B). Draw a logic diagram to represent this system, labelling both inputs and the output.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a single AND gate drawn with the recognised D-shaped symbol, both inputs (A and B) connected, and the output (Q) clearly labelled. Secure: correct gate and connections with a minor labelling omission. Developing: correct gate chosen but the diagram or labels are incomplete. Emerging: the wrong gate, or no recognisable logic diagram.

practice_questions.text: A heating system turns on (Q = 1) when the temperature is low (A = 1) OR the manual override is pressed (B = 1), but only while the system has power (C = 1). The system can be written as Q = (A OR B) AND C. Explain, step by step, how you would work out the output for the inputs A = 1, B = 0, C = 1.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: works out A OR B = 1 first (because at least one input is 1), then combines that result with C using AND to reach Q = 1, explaining the reason at each step. Secure: reaches Q = 1 with mostly correct working. Developing: correct method but an error in one step, or thin explanation. Emerging: an incorrect final result, or no clear working shown.

practice_questions.text: A security light (output Q) switches on when it is dark (A = 1) AND either motion is detected (B = 1) OR the manual switch is on (C = 1). Explain how logic gates and a truth table could be used to design and test this system. Refer to the gates needed, a suitable Boolean expression, and how the truth table would be built.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: identifies that an OR gate combines B and C, whose result is fed into an AND gate with A, giving the expression Q = A AND (B OR C); explains that the truth table needs 8 rows for the three inputs and describes using a helper column for B OR C before finding Q, so every case can be tested. Secure: correct gates and expression with a clear description of building the table. Developing: mostly correct gates or expression but the truth-table explanation is limited. Emerging: some relevant points but the logic or expression is largely incorrect.

practice_questions.text: State one characteristic of a high-level programming language.
practice_questions.marks: A correct response identifies a defining feature, such as: it uses English-like keywords; it is easy for people to read and write; one statement stands in for many machine instructions; it is portable across different machines; or it must be translated before it can run. A single clear characteristic gains the mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe one difference between a high-level language and a low-level language.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: a clear contrast made on the same measure — for example, that a high-level language uses English-like keywords and is portable across machines, whereas a low-level language is written closer to the hardware, is machine-specific and is harder for people to read. Developing: two unconnected facts about each language, or a difference only hinted at. Emerging: one vague or inaccurate point.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a program written in a high-level language needs a translator before it can run.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: explains that the processor can only execute machine code (binary), so a translator is needed to convert the high-level source code into machine code that the computer can run. One mark for identifying that the processor only understands machine code, a second for the point that the translator converts the code so it can be executed. Developing: states that code must be translated without saying why.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between how a compiler and an interpreter work.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two clear, correctly contrasted differences, each developed — for example, a compiler translates the whole program before it runs while an interpreter translates and runs one statement at a time; and a compiler produces a standalone executable while an interpreter needs the source code and interpreter present every time. Secure: two valid differences with some explanation. Developing: one difference explained, or two only stated. Emerging: a relevant point about either translator with limited accuracy.

practice_questions.text: Describe three tools that an Integrated Development Environment provides to help a programmer, and how each one helps.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: three distinct IDE tools, each with a brief note of how it helps — for example an editor (typing code with syntax highlighting and auto-indentation), error-diagnostic or debugging tools (breakpoints to pause and inspect the program), a run-time environment (running the program and viewing its output), or a built-in translator (converting the code so it can run). One mark per correctly described tool. Naming a tool without saying how it helps is developing.

practice_questions.text: A developer is writing and testing a new program and must decide whether to use a compiler or an interpreter. Discuss the benefits and drawbacks of each, and recommend which she should use while she is still developing the program.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a balanced discussion covering benefits and drawbacks of both translators, applied to the scenario, leading to a justified recommendation — for example, an interpreter during development because it stops at the first error and makes debugging quick, despite its slower running speed. Secure: clear benefits and drawbacks of both translators with a supported recommendation. Developing: some relevant points, mostly one-sided, with a limited or unsupported judgement. Emerging: a few basic points about either translator with no real comparison or conclusion.

practice_questions.text: State one function of an operating system.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating any one function, such as: providing a user interface; managing memory and multitasking; managing peripherals through drivers; managing users and access rights; or managing files.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by a user interface.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks. Creditable points: it is the part of the operating system that lets a user interact with the computer (1); for example a graphical interface using windows, icons, menus and a pointer, or a command line where text is typed (1). Secure: a clear description with an example. Developing: a basic definition with no example. Emerging: a vague reference to using the computer.

practice_questions.text: Explain how an operating system uses memory management to allow several programs to run at the same time.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks for a linked explanation: the operating system allocates an area of memory to each running program (1); it transfers data into and out of memory as each program is used (1); the processor is switched rapidly between the programs so they appear to run at the same time (1). Secure: a logical chain covering allocation and switching. Developing: correct facts but not fully linked. Emerging: an isolated point.

practice_questions.text: Explain two tasks that utility software carries out to keep a computer running smoothly.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks, up to 2 per task (1 for naming the task, 1 for explaining its purpose). Valid tasks: encryption (scrambles data with a key so it cannot be understood if stolen); defragmentation (reorganises scattered file parts so a drive reads faster); compression (reduces file size to save space and speed transfer). Secure: two tasks clearly explained. Developing: one task explained, or two named without explanation. Emerging: a single relevant point.

practice_questions.text: Explain how defragmentation software improves the performance of a hard disk drive.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a clear, well-sequenced explanation that over time file parts become scattered (fragmented) across the drive, that the moving read/write head must travel further to collect them, that defragmentation reorganises the drive so each file's parts are stored together, and that the head therefore moves less and files load faster. Secure: most of these steps explained in a sensible order. Developing: some correct points but gaps or muddled order. Emerging: knows defragmentation tidies the drive but cannot explain why it speeds things up.

practice_questions.text: A company stores confidential customer data on its computers, and staff report that the machines have become slow. Discuss how encryption software and defragmentation could help the company, and consider any drawbacks.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained discussion linking encryption to protecting confidential data so intercepted or stolen files cannot be read, linking defragmentation to reorganising scattered files so hard drives load faster, and weighing drawbacks such as encryption needing keys to be managed and defragmentation giving little benefit on solid state drives. Secure: several relevant, connected points covering both tools with at least one drawback. Developing: some correct points but limited linking or one-sided coverage. Emerging: isolated, partly correct points with no clear reasoning.

practice_questions.text: State two laws that help protect people when they use computers.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: any two of — the Data Protection Act 2018, the Computer Misuse Act 1990, the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 (1 mark each, maximum 2). Developing: one correct law named. Emerging: a vague reference to 'the law' with no named act.

practice_questions.text: Describe one difference between open source software and proprietary software.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: a clear difference, for example — open source makes its source code available so users can view and change it, whereas proprietary software keeps its source code secret so it cannot be changed (2). Developing: a correct point about one type only (1). Emerging: names the two types with no difference given.

practice_questions.text: A social media app collects users' personal data. Explain one privacy issue this could cause.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: identifies a privacy issue and explains its effect, e.g. the company stores personal data such as location and browsing habits (1); this data could be sold, leaked or stolen (1); so users lose control over who can see their private information (1). Developing: identifies a privacy issue with limited explanation. Emerging: a general comment that data is being collected.

practice_questions.text: A school stores personal data about its students. Describe two rules the Data Protection Act 2018 requires the school to follow.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: two rules, each described (2 marks each), chosen from — keep the data secure and protected; keep it accurate and up to date; use it only for the purpose it was collected; keep it no longer than necessary; allow students to see the data held about them. Developing: one rule described, or two rules named without description. Emerging: a vague statement that the school must 'follow the law'.

practice_questions.text: A small business is deciding whether to install open source or proprietary software on its office computers. Discuss the benefits and drawbacks of each and recommend which the business should choose.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a balanced discussion covering benefits and drawbacks of both — open source is free and can be customised but may lack official support; proprietary costs money and cannot be changed but comes with professional support and reliable updates — leading to a justified recommendation that suits a small business. Secure: benefits and drawbacks of both types with a clear recommendation. Developing: covers both types but one-sided, or gives a recommendation with weak reasons. Emerging: a few isolated points with little development.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the environmental impacts of the growing use of digital technology. Your answer should consider both positive and negative effects.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a balanced, well-developed discussion of negative effects (mining raw materials, the electricity used by devices and data centres, and e-waste sent to landfill) and positive effects (video calls and remote working reducing travel, smart devices cutting wasted energy, less need for paper), reaching a reasoned overall judgement. Secure: covers several negative and positive effects with clear explanation. Developing: covers effects on one side only, or several points with limited explanation. Emerging: one or two isolated points.
